strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (fine-grained and generic), backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and GCD baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) with extensive ablation studies
Consistent empirical improvements on fine-grained datasets (+9.8% SimGCD on SSB) with thorough analysis including success/failure case studies and attention map visualizations
Practical plug-and-play design that integrates seamlessly into existing GCD methods without architectural modifications
Clear motivation and well-articulated problem of why part-level information is needed beyond global [CLS] tokens, particularly for fine-grained categories
Honest assessment of limitations and failure modes, with detailed discussion of when part-level cues help (part-dependent classes) vs. hurt (global shape-dependent classes)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (PCA + k-means + contrastive learning) applied to GCD; no new methodological insights or algorithms introduced

Marginal improvements on generic datasets (CIFAR10/100/ImageNet: +0.3%/+0.9% for SimGCD, +2.2%/+1.0% for SelEx) undermines claims of broad applicability; method appears narrowly suited to fine-grained settings

Ad-hoc design choices with insufficient justification: foreground threshold τ_obj=0.6 (no ablation), double PCA application (vague motivation), k-selection criterion (unmotivated heuristic), using only M labeled samples for PCA (no sensitivity analysis)
Part label quality concerns: only 80.8% (1st order) and 77.5% (2nd order) accuracy compared to ground-truth CUB parts; no ablation on how this ~20% label error impacts downstream performance
Sometimes underperformed by concurrent methods: PartCo-SelEx (85.5%) vs. Hyp-SelEx (86.0%) on SSB; unclear why practitioners should choose PartCo when alternatives are available

Significant failure cases with up to -35% performance drops on certain classes with no adaptive mechanism to predict when method will help or hurt; practitioners cannot reliably determine applicability
Non-negligible computational overhead: 5-180 minutes label construction, +39% peak memory (8.6GB→12.0GB), +2.5-5% training time; gains on generic datasets don't justify this cost
Missing critical ablations: sensitivity to M (number of labeled samples), foreground threshold τ_obj, and label quality impact; incomplete comparison with related part-based methods (APL, PartGCD)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations across 6 datasets, 20+ baselines, and multiple backbones; strong fine-grained performance with +9.8% improvement on SSB fine-grained datasets
Practical plug-and-play design seamlessly integrates with multiple GCD methods without modifying architecture or inference path; adds only 5-15% training overhead
Well-motivated problem clearly articulated; honest failure case analysis distinguishing when part-level cues help (part-dependent classes) vs. hurt (global shape-biased classes)
Extensive supplementary material with additional datasets (Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19), CLIP backbone experiments, and detailed per-class success/failure analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution uses standard techniques (PCA, k-means, supervised contrastive loss) applied sequentially without methodological innovation; insufficient for top-tier venue

Questionable dependency on frozen DINOv2 features; large performance gap between DINOv2 (+9.8%) and DINOv3 (+3.8%) improvements, and poor CLIP results (70.5% vs 86.0%), suggesting method exploits DINOv2-specific properties rather than discovering general principle

Unjustified label construction: objectness threshold τ_obj=0.6 is arbitrary with no ablation; k* selection criterion lacks theoretical grounding; only ~80% agreement with ground-truth CUB parts; no analysis confirming labels capture semantic parts vs. arbitrary PCA clusters

Unclear contribution source: cannot rigorously isolate whether gains come from part-level correspondence learning or merely additional supervision signal; no comparison with learned part label assignment; no analysis of PartCo labels with random backbones

Dataset-dependent tuning required: manual classification as 'fine-grained' vs 'generic' for 1st/2nd order selection using vague criterion ('subtle intra-class differences'); no automatic method proposed despite claiming seamless integration

Inconsistent and often negligible gains on generic datasets (CIFAR10: +0.3%, CIFAR100: +0.9%, ImageNet-100: +0.1%) contradicting claim to 'set new benchmarks'; some baselines show negative gains (SelEx Old: -0.4%)

Insufficient novelty given concurrent work: APL and PartGCD also explore part-level information for GCD; PartCo's distinction (frozen vs. learned features) not convincingly superior; no direct comparison provided
Overstated benchmark claim: Hyp-SelEx achieves 86.0% on SSB vs. PartCo-SelEx's 85.5%; NCGCD-SelEx and ConGCD-SelEx comparable; PartCo not overall best, contradicting title

Critical reproducibility and robustness gaps: label construction requires 5-180 minutes with no code release promised; CLIP backbone gap (15.5% absolute) unexplained; no sensitivity analysis on τ_obj, k*, λ_b; no ablation on PCA decomposition strategy

Cannot separate method from pretrained features: heavy reliance on frozen DINOv2 means success depends on pretrained quality; no evidence this approach works with other feature extractors or learned part assignments; undermines claim of principled method contribution

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (fine-grained and generic), baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx), and backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP) with consistent improvements on fine-grained datasets (+9.8%, +8.2%, +4.8%)
Practical plug-and-play integration with no architectural modifications or inference overhead, making it immediately useful for practitioners
Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine limitation of existing GCD methods that rely solely on global [CLS] representations

Thorough experimental rigor including detailed ablation studies (1st vs. 2nd order labels, projection dimensions, balancing factors), success/failure case analysis providing insights into when part-level cues help vs. hurt, and robustness testing with incorrect K estimation
Honest discussion of limitations and failure cases in main paper and supplementary material, acknowledging that method can degrade performance on global-shape-biased categories by up to 35%
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (attention maps, part-label visualizations), well-organized methodology, and extensive supplementary material addressing design choices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—the approach (PCA + k-means clustering + standard contrastive learning) is relatively straightforward without significant algorithmic innovation; part-level contrastive loss is standard supervised contrastive learning applied to parts

Multiple ad-hoc design choices lack justification: threshold τ_obj=0.6 for foreground/background is fixed without ablation; k-means selection criterion weighting is not explained; choice of PCA for label generation over other dimensionality reduction methods is not compared

Frozen part-level labels that never adapt during training; no exploration of learned label refinement as the model learns, despite label quality being imperfect (80.8% and 77.5% agreement with ground-truth CUB parts)
Substantially smaller improvements on generic datasets (+0.3-2.2%) compared to fine-grained (+4.8-9.8%), limiting general applicability; no clear guidance for practitioners on when to apply PartCo
No comparison to concurrent part-based GCD methods (APL, PartGCD from 2025) despite mentioning them—unclear how PartCo empirically compares to these alternative approaches
Missing statistical significance testing (error bars, confidence intervals) and no specification of number of runs—particularly important given small improvements on generic datasets (+0.3%)
Non-trivial label construction overhead (5-180 minutes) despite being training-only, and hyperparameter selection (k-means candidate set) not fully specified

Limited insight into why frozen PCA-based labels work—lack of ablation on alternative label construction methods, and qualitative attention map analysis without quantitative verification that PartCo attends to semantically meaningful parts
